issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of frustration in Indian law is governed by the statutory rule on supervening impossibility, which includes practical impossibility and is distinct from discharge under an express or implied contractual term.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether a later government requisition discharged an agreement to sell land.
The agreement required the seller to construct roads and drains before the conveyance, but did not specify a completion deadline.
The Court considered whether the later event had fundamentally undermined the basis of the agreement.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of frustration is part of the law of discharge for supervening impossibility or illegality under section 56 of the Indian Contract Act. Impossibility is not confined to literal or physical impossibility; practical impossibility may suffice when an unexpected event fundamentally destroys the contract’s basis. Where the contract itself provides for discharge on an event, the matter is governed by the contract and section 32 or other applicable provisions, rather than section 56. English decisions are persuasive only.
issues.legal_principle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, sections 56, 32 and 9. The Court relied on Ganga Saran v. Ram Charan and Kesari Chand v. Governor-General in Council for the application of sections 32 and 56, and referred to Joseph Constantine Steamship Co. v. Imperial Smelting Corporation Ltd., Taylor v. Caldwell, and Denny, Mott and Dickson Ltd. v. James B. Fraser & Co. Ltd. in discussing the doctrine and its English formulations.

rule.if: contract_dispute and unexpected_supervening_event and fundamental_basis_destroyed and (performance_practically_impossible or performance_unlawful) and not contract_itself_provides_for_discharge

predicates.contract_dispute: The parties dispute whether a contract was discharged after it was made.
predicates.unexpected_supervening_event: An event occurred after the contract was made that the parties had not contemplated.
predicates.fundamental_basis_destroyed: The later event destroyed the fundamental basis or underlying object of the contract.
predicates.performance_practically_impossible: The promised act became impracticable or useless in light of the contract’s object, even if it remained literally possible.
predicates.performance_unlawful: The promised act became unlawful because of the later event.
predicates.contract_itself_provides_for_discharge: The parties expressly or impliedly agreed that the contract would end if the relevant event occurred.

issues.definition: When an unexpected later event fundamentally destroys the contract’s basis and makes performance practically impossible or unlawful, the contract is discharged on that ground unless the contract itself provides for discharge.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of frustration can apply to an agreement for the sale of land in India because the agreement does not itself transfer an interest in the land to the buyer.
material_facts: The agreement was for the sale of a plot of land.
The buyer was to receive a conveyance after the seller completed roads and drains and the balance of the price was paid.
The agreement had not resulted in a conveyance before the requisition orders.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of frustration is applicable in India to agreements for the sale of land, as it is to other agreements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that a contract for the sale of immovable property does not of itself create an interest in or charge on that property. The Court distinguished the English rule, under which a completed agreement to sell may make the buyer the equitable owner, and held that the Indian-law basis for excluding land-sale agreements from frustration therefore does not apply.

rule.if: agreement_for_sale_of_land and no_conveyance_completed and buyer_has_no_property_interest_before_conveyance and supervening_event_affects_performance

predicates.agreement_for_sale_of_land: The parties made an agreement under which one party would convey land to the other.
predicates.no_conveyance_completed: The promised conveyance had not been completed when the later event occurred.
predicates.buyer_has_no_property_interest_before_co: The buyer had not acquired an interest in the land merely by making the agreement to buy it.
predicates.supervening_event_affects_performance: A later event affected the parties’ ability to perform the agreement.

issues.definition: When an agreement to sell land remains uncompleted by conveyance and the buyer has not acquired a property interest under the agreement, a later event affecting performance does not by itself prevent application of the frustration doctrine.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary government requisition did not frustrate the land-sale agreement where it did not destroy the agreement’s fundamental basis or make performance impossible.
material_facts: The agreement formed part of a development scheme for residential plots and required the seller to build roads and drains before conveyance.
The agreement set no time limit for completing that work, and there was no understanding between the parties about a completion date.
War conditions existed when the agreement was made, and the seller had not begun development work when the first requisition order was made.
The government requisitioned portions of the land for military purposes; the requisition was temporary in nature.
The seller said the work could not proceed for an indefinite period and sought to treat the agreement as cancelled.
issues.conclusion: The requisition did not affect the fundamental basis of the agreement or make its performance impossible within section 56, so the agreement was not frustrated.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the Court assesses whether the actual later circumstances made performance impossible in the practical sense or destroyed the contract’s basis. It considered the nature and terms of the agreement, the circumstances in which it was made, the absence of a completion deadline, the existing war conditions, the scale of the development work, and the temporary character of the requisition. The Court also referred to Joseph Constantine Steamship Co. v. Imperial Smelting Corporation Ltd. and Denny, Mott and Dickson Ltd. v. James B. Fraser & Co. Ltd. on assessing the effect of what actually happened on performance.

rule.if: land_sale_contract_dispute and development_work_promised_before_conveyance and no_fixed_completion_deadline and war_conditions_known_when_contract_made and temporary_requisition_occupies_some_land and not fundamental_basis_destroyed

predicates.land_sale_contract_dispute: The parties dispute whether an agreement for the sale of land was discharged.
predicates.development_work_promised_before_conveya: The seller promised to complete development work before conveying the land.
predicates.no_fixed_completion_deadline: The agreement set no deadline for completing the promised work.
predicates.war_conditions_known_when_contract_made: War conditions already existed when the parties made the agreement.
predicates.temporary_requisition_occupies_some_land: The government temporarily took possession of some of the land for public purposes.
predicates.fundamental_basis_destroyed: The later event destroyed the fundamental basis or underlying object of the contract.

issues.definition: A land-sale agreement requiring development work before conveyance is not frustrated by a temporary requisition of some land where there is no fixed completion deadline and the requisition does not destroy the agreement’s fundamental basis.

issues.legal_issue: A contention that government requisition made contractual performance unlawful should not be considered when it is raised for the first time on appeal and requires examination of matters not previously raised.
material_facts: The respondent argued in the Supreme Court that the requisition made performance unlawful and the agreement void.
That contention had not been raised in the courts below or indicated in the respondent’s statement of the case.
Resolving it would require consideration of provisions governing the requisition and the implications of an illustration to the Contract Act.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the respondent to raise the illegality contention for the first time before it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that it would not be proper to permit a new contention requiring examination of statutory provisions and related implications when that contention had not been raised in the courts below or identified in the statement of the case.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party raises a contention in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.contention_not_raised_below: The party did not raise that contention in the courts below.
predicates.contention_requires_new_legal_examinatio: Deciding the contention requires examination of legal provisions or implications not previously considered.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a contention not raised below is not considered when deciding it requires new legal examination.
